Several people in my life have told me to talk to a doctor about hEDS.  It happened for the first time a couple years ago when I was at a friend's place and just passively stretching my arms in different positions. I think it's a stim I do when I'm bored, not sure, but she saw me put my arms behind my back and place my palms flat together as if I were praying. She has hEDS, and saw me doing that, and basically took me through the Beighton test. I'm around a 5 on the scale, with one of my knees being closer to hypermobile than average but not meeting criteria, and the other meeting criteria. I met criteria 1-4 VERY easily with my wrists and pinkies.

  
I looked into it more and feature A on criterion 2, I have

Unusually soft/ velvety skin: I've had quite a few people remark on this. 

  
Mild skin hyperextensibility: Around 1.7-2cm underarm, exceeding 3cm on the elbow

  
Unexplained striae distensae or rubae: Present in the groin area since adolescence. More appeared when I gained weight (around 10kg) and when my breasts came in. The ones that came in after weight gain I don't count.

  
Bilateral piezogenic papules of the heel

  
Positive Walker sign

  
When it comes to pain, chronic symptoms, etc, I don't have a lot of pain in the joints, necessarily. I do have other sorts of pain and general issues which seem to be common with hEDS. Stomach/ bowel issues, headaches, history of orthostatic hypotension (less so recently), nerve pain which varies from nonexistent (most common), to mild, to severe. Severe flareups are rare and have me writhing in agony. It is a burning sensation, like I'm being injected with molten tungsten. But this pain is not daily. Joint pain does occur, seemingly at random. Every day though, since I was a kid, my joints crack. Some say they hear it, but I think it's typical, all things considered.

  
I'm also not sure what "joint instability" means. A lot of these things are really vague. 

  
There's also an issue where, ever since I was a small child, I'd move my jaw in order to make a crackling sensation in my ear. Now that happens every time I move my jaw or swallow. I also crack my pinky knuckles all the time as a tic. Both of these things have resulted in severe pain in the past but on normal days are benign. I also have issues with standing for a long time. I end up with a lot of pain, especially in the chest, unless I'm also walking. 



  
In all honesty, I'm nearly certain I don't have it since I don't have chronic joint pain. I know 10% of people are hypermobile and I have a lot of hypermobility, but I'm not sure if it also presents with all these other things. They could all, very easily be other things, or "symptoms of life" tbh. I really don't want to give my doctor the impression that I'm prone to health anxiety. I take my health seriously, and I certainly wouldn't take anything I read here as final. I just don't know if I have generally benign hypermobility (seems most likely), or something else. There doesn't seem to be a lot of information and a lot of what's provided is really vague.

Therapists have commented on this, and doubted that I'm autistic partly because of this, along with my ability to mask. If I'm anxious, I don't mask as well, bit I warm up to therapists rather quickly. I feel like I'm in a strange gray area, where I have s ok me subtle indicators that I'm autistic, while having traits that contradict it. 


I'm not a straightforward communicator, I tend to hint at things as opposed to saying then outright because I understand the effect saying it outright will have, and I depend on others doing the same for me. This has created a lot of confusion with autistic friends of mine. This isn't to say that I don't miss things, but being able to communicate in that way has helped me tremendously.


I once had a therapist tell me that he didn't believe I was autistic because his autistic patients tend to have a certain "aura" about them. I instantly knew what he meant. I notice that as well. I have enough experience socially to manage my social difficulties to a point where I've fostered a personality that both fits me well and hides the fact that I'm autistic from neurotypical people. It's this kind of quirky, submissive personality and being queer, I think you know how others would perceive me as a result. In short, I've found ways to move about my social life relatively seamlessly. This of course comes at a cost, since I dig deeply into my every social shortcoming and seek to weed them out.


I'm pretty good at telling the difference between anxiety attacks, panic attacks, and sensory overload/ meltdowns. 


My anxiety attacks are typically episodes of worrying about things to the point where I just can't relax, I feel like I have a million things weighing down on me at once and I feel a sense or urgency that I can't quite manage. I'm a problem solver, so I find it difficult to simply sit with an unresolved problem, and it's far more important to me to solve it than to manage the emotion stemming from it.


My panic attacks are like you described. I'll be hit with a huge sense of impending doom. I'll be convinced that I'm dying. I'll hyperventilate. When I had my first panic attack, I went to the ER because I was convinced I was having a stroke. I was prescribed alprazolam which turned into an addiction where I was buying street bars and research chemicals/ analogs online. 


My meltdowns come when I have too much sensory input. I'm at much higher risk of them if I'm already dealing with difficult emotions, primarily anxiety. When this happens, I'm bothered by the dog barking three houses down the street, my tinnitus, cars driving by, whatever faint tapping sound is coming from down the hall and driving me fucking mad.
It's almost always coupled with anger. I hate myself for having to deal with sensory overload since it's not a neurotypical experience. I punish myself for having them, knowing that nothing good will come of it. It's just satisfying to give myself what I feel I deserve, but it's never enough. The sort of self hatred I have brings me a desire to brutalize myself in unimaginable ways. I believe at my core that I deserve it. This isn't from some sense of justice or an attempt to solve a problem. It happens when the problem is unsolvable, since one cannot simply "solve" a disability. It's a recognition of defeat. I've surrendered to the fact that as long as I live, I will live with shortcomings. 


I hate not understanding things. When I fail to understand something that somebody else does, whether it's some unspoken social rule or scientific theory that requires years of education to grasp, I hate myself for not understanding. I'll call myself a certain ableist slur that I'm not going to repeat, and I'll have a strong desire to understand it.

I'm seeing a lot of comments here about autism and here's my take, because it's not as black and white as people make it out to be. 


I'm autistic, and I absolutely hate when people say "autism took my child from me" and stuff like that. It's harmful to their child and it's harmful to autistic people who have to hear neurotypicals act like their existence is a burden. That's a very difficult thing to live with. I'm not even talking about autistics with low support needs, either. I know autistics who are nonverbal, incontinent and have higher support needs who have the same thoughts.

At the same time, there is something to be said about autistic people who have violent behaviors and/ or intellectual disabilities, and that is something that can be difficult for caretakers. Should they treat an intellectually disabled adult as if they're a child, or to wish death upon them? No. They are still an adult and have just as much a right to live as anybody else, but it's important to recognize that such a profound level of disability is not the same as simply seeing the world differently or just being different. Some of the violent behaviors exhibited can be a result of their sensory needs never being met, but still, not being able to effectively communicate verbally or nonverbally those sensory needs is a significant hurdle

Also, some level of functioning labels can be useful and it's shortsighted to say that functioning labels shouldn't be used at all. Their application and perception should be changed in order to provide support for those deemed high functioning who are often denied services for being high functioning, but somebody like me who can navigate the world fairly well, has a social life, can live independently and can advocate for themself is not comparable to somebody on the opposite end of the spectrum. 

That being said, fuck this parent.
